en: The Philippine eagle raises its distinctive, shaggy brown crest feathers when alarmed, making it highly visible in the forest canopy.
Our national flower, the Sampaguita, blooms year-round and releases its strongest sweet scent at night to attract moth pollinators.
The Ifugao people built the Banaue Rice Terraces by carving mountains and using forest-top springs for gravity-fed irrigation.
During the Pahiyas Festival, locals decorate homes with kiping, which are colorful, leaf-shaped wafers made from pounded rice.
Ancient Filipinos built the Balangay boats by stitching wooden planks together using strong, flexible plant fibers.
The Tagalog word amihan refers to the observable northeast monsoon that brings cool, dry air to the Philippines.
T'boli weavers create T'nalak cloth by extracting and drying strong fibers from the leaf sheaths of abaca plants.
National hero Jose Rizal cultivated and studied various medicinal plants in Dapitan to treat local residents for free.
Scientist Dr. Fe del Mundo designed a rural newborn incubator using local bamboo and hot water bottles.
Our national fish, the milkfish, has no teeth and uses specialized gill rakers to filter microscopic algae from coastal water.
The Department of Environment and Natural Resources enforces laws to protect coastal mangrove forests from illegal logging and pollution.
The Philippine Carabao mango, our national fruit, changes from green to yellow when it ripens due to chlorophyll breakdown.
